{{Orphan|date=December 2022}}

A '''universal Taylor series''' is a [[formal power series]] <math>\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n</math>, such that for every continuous function <math>h</math> on <math>[-1,1]</math>, if <math>h(0)=0</math>, then there exists an increasing sequence <math>\left(\lambda_n\right)</math> of positive integers such that<math display="block">
\lim_{n\to\infty}\left\|\sum_{k=1}^{\lambda_n} a_k x^k-h(x)\right\| = 0
</math>In other words, the set of partial sums of <math>\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n x^n</math> is dense (in [[Uniform norm|sup-norm]]) in <math>C[-1,1]_0</math>, the set of continuous functions on <math>[-1,1]</math> that is zero at origin.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mouze |first1=A. |last2=Nestoridis |first2=V. |date=2010 |title=Universality and ultradifferentiable functions: Fekete's theorem |url=https://www.ams.org/proc/2010-138-11/S0002-9939-10-10380-3/ |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=138 |issue=11 |pages=3945–3955 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-10-10380-3 |issn=0002-9939|doi-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Statements and proofs ==
[[Michael Fekete|Fekete]] proved that a universal Taylor series exists.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pál |first=Julius |date=1914 |title=Zwei kleine Bemerkungen |url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/tmj1911/6/0/6_0_42/_article/-char/ja/ |journal=Tohoku Mathematical Journal |series=First Series |volume=6 |pages=42–43}}</ref>
{{Math proof|title=Proof|proof=Let <math>f_1, f_2, ...</math> be the sequence in which each rational-coefficient polynomials with zero constant coefficient appears countably infinitely many times (use the [[Pairing_function#Cantor_pairing_function|diagonal enumeration]]). By [[Weierstrass theorem on polynomial approximation|Weierstrass approximation theorem]], it is dense in <math>C[-1,1]_0</math>. Thus it suffices to approximate the sequence. We construct the power series iteratively as a sequence of polynomials <math>p_1, p_2, ...</math>, such that <math>p_n, p_{n+1}</math> agrees on the first <math>n</math> coefficients, and <math>\|f_n - p_n \|_\infty \leq 1/n</math>.

To start, let <math>p_1 = f_1</math>. To construct <math>p_{n+1}</math>, replace each <math>x</math> in <math>f_{n+1} - p_n</math> by a close enough approximation with lowest degree <math>\geq n+1</math>, using the lemma below. Now add this to <math>p_n</math>.}}

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = The function <math>f(x) = x</math> can be approximated to arbitrary precision with a polynomial with arbitrarily lowest degree. That is, <math>\forall \epsilon > 0, n \in \{1, 2, ...\}\exists </math> polynomial <math>p(x) = a_nx^n + \cdots + a_N x^N,</math> such that <math>\|f-p\|_\infty \leq \epsilon</math>.
| name = Lemma
| note = 
}}

{{Math proof|title=Proof of lemma|proof=The function <math>g(x) = x - c\tanh (x/c)</math> is the uniform limit of its Taylor expansion, which starts with degree 3. Also, <math>\|f-g\|_\infty < c</math>. Thus to <math>\epsilon</math>-approximate <math>f(x) =x</math> using a polynomial with lowest degree 3, we do so for <math>g(x)</math> with <math>c < \epsilon/2</math> by truncating its Taylor expansion. Now iterate this construction by plugging in the lowest-degree-3 approximation into the Taylor expansion of <math>g(x)</math>, obtaining an approximation of lowest degree 9, 27, 81...}}
